title: A devastating case of a Balamuthia mandrillaris pediatric brain infection
case_prompt: A 3-year-old Hispanic boy in Arizona with a baseline right facial palsy presented with 5 days of fatigue, abdominal pain, and right cheek pain. Outpatient treatment for presumed otitis and sinusitis with ear drops and penicillin yielded no improvement. He then developed intermittent fevers, speech changes, gait instability, and difficulty sitting up. A rapid Group A Streptococcus test was positive, and penicillin was changed to cephalexin. The next day, he had seizure-like activity unresponsive to voice and received midazolam en route to the Emergency Department. On arrival he was febrile, had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8, and altered mental status. He experienced a generalized tonic–clonic seizure treated with lorazepam and levetiracetam. Noncontrast head CT showed hypoattenuation consistent with edema in the right frontal and left frontoparietal lobes. He was started on ceftriaxone and vancomycin. Admission laboratory studies showed a normal metabolic panel, WBC 10.1 K/μL, hemoglobin 14.4 g/dL, and platelets 321 K/μL. CSF obtained by lumbar puncture demonstrated 75 WBC/μL, 5 RBC/μL, glucose 53 mg/dL, and protein 85 mg/dL. A multiplex CSF PCR panel was negative for bacterial, viral, and fungal pathogens. Pending studies included CSF oligoclonal bands, serum aquaporin-4 receptor antibody, and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody. Empirical dexamethasone and IV immunoglobulin were begun. After transfer to the PICU, he was intubated without sedation and lacked brainstem reflexes. EEG showed diffuse slowing consistent with moderate encephalopathy. MRI four days after admission revealed extensive bilateral supratentorial and infratentorial diffusion restriction, T2 hyperintensity, necrosis, subarachnoid and parenchymal enhancement, and patchy frontal-lobe involvement. A follow-up MRI three days later showed marked progression of diffusion restriction and T2 FLAIR hyperintensity with increased involvement of the periventricular regions, cerebellum, basal nuclei, thalami, brainstem, leptomeninges, and petechial hemorrhages.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial meningitis — “CSF analysis by ARUP meningitis/encephalitis PCR panel was negative for bacterial, viral, and fungal DNA ... These results made bacterial, viral, and fungal meningitis less likely.”  
2. Viral encephalitis — “CSF analysis by ARUP meningitis/encephalitis PCR panel was negative for bacterial, viral, and fungal DNA ... These results made bacterial, viral, and fungal meningitis less likely.”  
3. Fungal meningitis — “CSF analysis by ARUP meningitis/encephalitis PCR panel was negative for bacterial, viral, and fungal DNA ... These results made bacterial, viral, and fungal meningitis less likely.”  
4. Multiple sclerosis — “Additional tests included pending CSF oligoclonal bands (elevated in multiple sclerosis and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis)…”  
5. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis — “Additional tests included pending CSF oligoclonal bands (elevated in multiple sclerosis and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis)…”  
6. Neuromyelitis optica — “Additional tests included … serum aquaporin-4 receptor (diagnostic for neuromyelitis optica)…”  
7. MOG antibody disease — “Additional tests included … myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody (seen in myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody disease [MOGAD]).”  
8. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis — “Differential diagnoses include viral or bacterial meningoencephalitis, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, toxoplasmosis, or neurocysticercosis.”  
9. Toxoplasmosis — “Differential diagnoses include viral or bacterial meningoencephalitis, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, toxoplasmosis, or neurocysticercosis.”  
10. Neurocysticercosis — “Differential diagnoses include viral or bacterial meningoencephalitis, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, toxoplasmosis, or neurocysticercosis.”
